title: Accutane and Alcohol: Can You Drink on Isotretinoin?
excerpt: Can you drink on Accutane? How isotretinoin and alcohol both raise triglycerides and stress the liver, how much is too much, what it does to your bloodwork, and when to call a doctor.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Accutane? How isotretinoin and alcohol affect your liver, triglycerides, and bloodwork, plus dryness tips and when to call a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** isotretinoin (the drug most people still call Accutane) doesn't cause a dangerous instant reaction with alcohol the way a few antibiotics do. One drink is not going to poison you. The real problem is that isotretinoin and alcohol lean on the same two things: your **liver** and the **fats in your blood (triglycerides)**. Both can rise on isotretinoin, and alcohol pushes both of them up too. That's why most dermatologists ask you to avoid alcohol or keep it to a minimum during treatment, and why a heavy weekend can show up on your next blood test. This guide explains what's actually going on, how much is too much, what to expect from your monthly labs, and when to call your doctor.

**The quick rules:** Ask your dermatologist what limit they want you to follow, because it depends on your bloodwork. If you do drink, keep it to an occasional drink or two, never binge, and skip alcohol for at least a couple of days before a blood test. Drink extra water, because isotretinoin already dries you out. If your doctor has told you your triglycerides or liver enzymes are high, don't drink at all until they say it's fine.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and prescribing guidance. It is not a substitute for the dermatologist who prescribed your isotretinoin and knows your blood results. **Call your doctor if** you've been told your triglycerides or liver enzymes are raised, you drink most days, you have diabetes, obesity, or a family history of high cholesterol, or you have a history of depression. **Get urgent care right away if** you have severe stomach pain that spreads to your back (with or without vomiting), yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, a severe headache with blurred vision, or thoughts of harming yourself. In an emergency, call 911. In the US, you can call or text **988** for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at any time.

## Why Accutane and Alcohol Don't Mix: The Interaction in Plain Words

Accutane was the original brand name for **isotretinoin**. The brand itself was discontinued in the US in 2009, but the drug lives on under names like Absorica, Claravis, Amnesteem, Zenatane, and Myorisan. Everything in this guide applies to all of them, because the active ingredient is the same.

Isotretinoin is a form of vitamin A. It shrinks the oil glands in your skin, which is why it works so well on severe acne. But it doesn't only act on your skin. It also changes how your body handles fats and puts some extra load on your liver. Alcohol does both of those things too. So the issue isn't a sudden chemical clash in your glass. It's two things stacking on top of each other over weeks.

### Problem 1: Triglycerides

Triglycerides are the main type of fat carried in your blood. Isotretinoin commonly raises them. The US prescribing information reports that about a quarter of patients in clinical trials had higher triglycerides on the drug, and some saw drops in "good" HDL cholesterol or rises in total cholesterol. In rare cases, triglyceride levels have climbed very high.

Alcohol raises triglycerides on its own. Your liver turns some of the alcohol you drink into fat, and a heavy session can push triglycerides up for a while afterward. The prescribing information lists **increased alcohol intake** as one of the things that makes someone more likely to develop high triglycerides on isotretinoin, alongside diabetes, obesity, and inherited lipid problems.

Why does this matter? Very high triglycerides can cause **pancreatitis**, a painful and sometimes serious inflammation of the pancreas. Heavy drinking is also one of the most common causes of pancreatitis in its own right. Pancreatitis on isotretinoin is rare, but the prescribing information does warn about it, and it's the main reason doctors watch your lipid results closely.

### Problem 2: Your liver

Your liver processes both isotretinoin and alcohol. The prescribing information notes that mild to moderate rises in liver enzymes were seen in roughly 15% of people in clinical trials, and that hepatitis possibly linked to the drug has been reported. Most of these enzyme bumps are small and go away, sometimes without stopping the drug.

Alcohol is one of the most common reasons liver enzymes go up in otherwise healthy people. Drinking heavily, or even just drinking a lot the weekend before your blood test, can raise markers like ALT, AST, and GGT. Your doctor then has a harder job: is the drug irritating your liver, or was it the party? That uncertainty can lead to a lower dose, a pause in treatment, or repeat tests.

### Problem 3: Dryness and dehydration

Dryness is the side effect almost everyone on isotretinoin gets: cracked lips, dry skin, dry eyes, and sometimes nosebleeds. Alcohol makes you pee more and can leave you dehydrated. Neither one is dangerous on its own, but together they can make your lips split, your eyes sting, and your hangovers feel rougher than they used to.

### Problem 4: Mood

Isotretinoin's label carries warnings about depression, mood changes, and, rarely, suicidal thoughts. Whether the drug actually causes these is still debated, but doctors take the warning seriously. Alcohol is a depressant, it disrupts sleep, and the day after heavy drinking often brings low mood and anxiety. If your mood has dipped during treatment, alcohol is likely to make it worse, not better.

## What Dermatologists and Official Guidance Say

There isn't one universal rule, and you'll hear different things from different doctors. Here's the general picture:

- **The prescribing information doesn't ban alcohol outright,** but it does flag alcohol as a risk factor for high triglycerides and asks doctors to monitor blood fats and liver function.
- **Many dermatologists advise avoiding alcohol entirely** during the course, mainly to keep your blood results clean and your liver workload low.
- **Others allow light, occasional drinking** for patients whose labs are normal, with clear instructions not to binge.
- **Almost all of them will tell you to stop** if your triglycerides or liver enzymes start rising.

The practical takeaway is that your own blood results decide this, not a general rule from the internet. If your dermatologist hasn't said anything about alcohol, ask at your next appointment. It's a normal question and they hear it constantly.

## Can You Drink on Accutane at All?

For many people with normal bloodwork, an occasional drink is unlikely to cause harm. But "can" and "should" aren't the same thing here, and a few groups should not drink at all during treatment:

- People whose **triglycerides are already raised** on their blood tests
- People whose **liver enzymes are raised**
- People with **diabetes, obesity, or a family history of high cholesterol or triglycerides**
- Anyone who has had **pancreatitis** before
- Anyone whose **mood has dropped** since starting treatment

If you're not in any of those groups and your dermatologist is fine with it, the safer pattern looks like this: one or two drinks on an occasional night, with food, with water alongside, and never on consecutive days. The pattern that causes trouble is the opposite: drinking most nights, or saving it all up for one heavy session.

## How Much Alcohol Is Too Much on Accutane?

Nobody can give you a safe number that fits everyone, and you should be wary of any website that does. What we can say:

| Situation | General guidance |
|---|---|
| Normal labs, dermatologist OK with light drinking | Occasional, light drinking (one or two drinks) with food. No binges. Not on back-to-back days. |
| Triglycerides raised on bloodwork | Most doctors will ask you not to drink. Alcohol directly raises triglycerides. |
| Liver enzymes raised on bloodwork | Avoid alcohol until your doctor says otherwise. |
| A blood test in the next couple of days | Skip alcohol so your results reflect the drug, not the weekend. |
| History of pancreatitis, diabetes, or lipid problems | Talk to your doctor before drinking at all. |

A "standard drink" in the US is about 14 grams of alcohol: roughly a 12-ounce regular beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine, or a 1.5-ounce shot of spirits. Many cocktails, craft beers, and generous wine pours are more than one. Counting honestly matters more than usual while you're on isotretinoin.

**Binge drinking is the real risk.** Four or five drinks in one sitting gives your liver and blood fats a much bigger jolt than the same amount spread across a week. If you only remember one thing from this guide, make it that.

## Your Monthly Bloodwork: Why Drinking Before a Blood Test Matters

Most people on isotretinoin have blood taken before starting and then again during the course. In the US, people who can get pregnant also have monthly pregnancy tests through the iPLEDGE program. Lipid and liver testing schedules vary. Some dermatologists test monthly, and others test at the start and once or twice early on, because several studies have questioned whether frequent lab tests are needed for healthy patients whose early results are normal.

Whatever your schedule, these are the numbers your doctor is watching:

- **Triglycerides**, the blood fat that isotretinoin and alcohol both raise
- **Total cholesterol and HDL**, which can shift on the drug
- **Liver enzymes (ALT and AST)**, which can rise from the drug, from alcohol, and from hard exercise

Alcohol in the day or two before a test can raise triglycerides and liver enzymes enough to make your results look worse than they really are. That can lead to a repeat test, a lower dose, or a pause in treatment you didn't need.

**Before a blood test, a sensible routine is:**

1. Skip alcohol for at least two to three days beforehand, or longer if your doctor prefers.
2. Follow your doctor's fasting instructions. Many lipid tests are done fasting, and a big meal the night before can raise triglycerides too.
3. Avoid an unusually hard workout the day before. Intense exercise can raise some muscle and liver markers on its own.
4. Be honest with your doctor about what you drank. They can read your results better if they know.

## Accutane, Alcohol, and Dry Lips, Skin, and Eyes

Dryness is the side effect that makes drinking on isotretinoin noticeably less pleasant. Alcohol pulls water out of your body, and isotretinoin has already reduced the oil that normally protects your skin and lips. Some people find their lips crack and bleed after a night out in a way they never did before treatment.

What helps:

- **Alternate every drink with a glass of water.** It slows your drinking down and offsets some of the fluid loss.
- **Keep a thick lip balm with you**, and reapply before bed. Petroleum jelly or a dermatologist-recommended balm works better than flavored glosses.
- **Use lubricating eye drops** if your eyes feel gritty, especially in smoky or dry bars. Contact lens wearers often find lenses harder to tolerate on isotretinoin.
- **Run a humidifier** at night if your room is dry.
- **Rehydrate properly the next morning.** Water plus some electrolytes helps more than water alone after a heavy night. Our guide to [when to take electrolytes around drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) covers the timing.

Nosebleeds are another common isotretinoin side effect from dry nasal lining. Alcohol widens blood vessels a little, so some people notice more nosebleeds after drinking. A saline nasal spray or a dab of petroleum jelly inside the nostrils can help.

## Are Hangovers Worse on Accutane?

A lot of people say yes. There isn't good research measuring hangovers on isotretinoin specifically, but it makes sense based on what the drug does:

- You start out more dried out, so dehydration symptoms like headache and thirst hit harder.
- Isotretinoin can cause headaches, tiredness, and muscle and joint aches on its own. A hangover adds to all three.
- Dry eyes and lips feel worse the next day.
- If your mood is already lower than usual, the next-day anxiety and low mood that often follow drinking can feel heavier.

If your tolerance seems lower than before you started treatment, believe it and drink less.

### Be careful with hangover painkillers

Reaching for a painkiller the morning after is normal, but think about it a bit more carefully while you're on isotretinoin:

- **Acetaminophen (Tylenol)** is processed by the liver, the same organ your doctor is monitoring. A single standard dose is usually fine, but don't take more than the label allows, and check for hidden acetaminophen in cold and flu products. Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains the liver risk in detail.
- **Ibuprofen and other NSAIDs** are easier on the liver but harder on the stomach and kidneys, especially when you're dehydrated. Our [ibuprofen and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) covers this.

And a specific warning: a **severe headache that doesn't go away, especially with blurred vision, nausea, or vomiting**, is not a hangover on isotretinoin. It can be a sign of raised pressure around the brain, a rare but serious side effect. The risk is higher if you also take a tetracycline antibiotic like doxycycline or minocycline, which shouldn't be combined with isotretinoin. Call your doctor that day.

## Accutane and Alcohol After Treatment: How Long to Wait

Isotretinoin leaves your body fairly quickly. Its half-life (the time it takes your body to clear half of it) is around a day, so most of the drug is gone within about a week of your last dose. Raised triglycerides and liver enzymes usually return to normal after the course ends.

There isn't an official waiting period for alcohol after isotretinoin. A reasonable approach:

- **Wait until your doctor has confirmed your final blood results are normal**, if you had any raised numbers during treatment.
- If your labs stayed normal throughout, many people return to their usual drinking within a week or two after finishing. Ask your dermatologist if you're unsure.
- Remember that **iPLEDGE contraception rules continue for one month after your last dose** for people who can get pregnant. That matters for the next point.

Your skin will usually stay dry for a few weeks after stopping, so the hydration tips above still apply.

## The Pregnancy Point Nobody Likes to Mention

Isotretinoin causes severe birth defects, even from a short exposure. That's why the US iPLEDGE program requires people who can get pregnant to use two forms of contraception, take monthly pregnancy tests, and keep using contraception for a month after the last dose.

Alcohol lowers inhibitions and makes it easier to forget a pill or skip a condom. This isn't a lecture, just a practical fact: if you drink while on isotretinoin, have your contraception sorted before you go out, not after. If you think you might be pregnant at any point, stop taking isotretinoin and call your doctor right away.

## Does Alcohol Make Accutane Less Effective?

There's no good evidence that moderate drinking stops isotretinoin from clearing acne. The drug works by shrinking oil glands, and alcohol doesn't block that.

What can happen is indirect. If drinking raises your liver enzymes or triglycerides, your dermatologist may lower your dose or pause treatment, and a lower or interrupted course can mean slower results or a longer course overall. So the main way alcohol can "get in the way" of your treatment is by complicating your blood tests.

On the skin side, alcohol can make your face flush and look puffy, and it may make redness and dryness look worse for a day or two. Our [guide to alcohol and skin health](/never-hungover/alcohol-skin-health-anti-aging-impact-analysis-2025) covers how drinking affects skin over time.

## Other Things to Watch on Accutane When You Go Out

A few isotretinoin side effects matter more when you're out drinking:

- **Night vision.** Isotretinoin can reduce your ability to see in the dark, and in some people this lasts. Combined with alcohol, that's another strong reason not to drive at night. (You shouldn't drive after drinking anyway.)
- **Sun sensitivity.** Your skin burns much more easily on isotretinoin. Daytime drinking at a beach, pool, or festival is a recipe for a bad burn, and alcohol makes you less likely to notice. Wear sunscreen and reapply.
- **Muscle and joint aches.** Isotretinoin can cause aches, and so can dehydration. Dancing all night on top of both can leave you very sore.
- **Previous antibiotics.** Many people take an antibiotic like doxycycline before moving to isotretinoin. If you're coming off one, our [antibiotics and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/antibiotics-and-alcohol) explains which ones actually clash with alcohol.

## Supplements While on Accutane: Check First

Many people look for something to "protect" their liver while on isotretinoin, especially if they plan to drink. Be careful here.

The most important rule: **don't take vitamin A supplements** while on isotretinoin. Isotretinoin is already a form of vitamin A, and doubling up raises the risk of vitamin A toxicity. Check multivitamins, "skin, hair, and nails" blends, and some hangover products for vitamin A or retinol on the label.

Beyond that, tell your dermatologist about any supplement you plan to take. Herbal liver products can affect liver enzymes themselves and make your blood results harder to read.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You're at higher risk from combining isotretinoin and alcohol if you:

- Already have **raised triglycerides or liver enzymes** on your bloodwork
- Have **diabetes, obesity, or a personal or family history of high cholesterol or triglycerides**
- Have had **pancreatitis** or have **liver disease**
- Usually drink **several drinks most days** or binge on weekends
- Have a history of **depression or anxiety**, or have noticed low mood during treatment
- Are also taking other medicines that affect the liver

If any of these describe you, have a short conversation with your dermatologist or pharmacist before drinking during treatment. For a wider look at how common medicines interact with alcohol and supplements, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## When to See a Doctor

Most people get through an isotretinoin course with nothing more than dry lips and a few borderline blood results. But call your doctor promptly, or get urgent care, if you notice any of these:

- **Severe stomach pain**, especially in the upper belly and spreading to your back, with or without nausea and vomiting. This can be a sign of pancreatitis and needs same-day care.
- **Yellowing of your skin or eyes, dark urine, or pale stools.** These can be signs of liver injury.
- **A severe or constant headache with blurred vision, nausea, or vomiting.**
- **Low mood that doesn't lift, losing interest in things, or thoughts of self-harm.** In the US, call or text 988 any time. If you're in danger, call 911.
- **Rectal bleeding, severe diarrhea, or stomach pain that won't settle.**
- **Any chance you might be pregnant.** Stop isotretinoin and call your doctor right away.

## A Smarter Approach If You Do Drink

If your dermatologist is fine with occasional light drinking, the goal is to keep the load on your liver and blood fats as low as possible:

- **Drink less and slower.** One or two drinks, spread out, with food.
- **Avoid binges and back-to-back nights.**
- **Hydrate more than you think you need to.** Your starting point is drier than usual.
- **Skip sugary mixers and big greasy late-night meals,** since both can push triglycerides higher.
- **Keep alcohol away from your blood test days.**

Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through the habits with the best evidence.

Some people also ask about hangover supplements. Here's an honest view. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies, with only a small amount of human data. There's no good evidence that DHM lowers triglycerides or liver enzymes in people taking isotretinoin, no research on combining the two, and it does not make drinking on isotretinoin safe. If you want to try it, clear it with your dermatologist first, and pick a simple single-ingredient product so you know exactly what you're taking and can confirm there's no added vitamin A. A plain option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), which is DHM on its own. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take, and our [best liver supplements guide](/never-hungover/best-liver-supplements) compares the evidence for other options. Just remember that while you're on isotretinoin, your doctor needs to know about anything that could affect your liver.

## The Bottom Line

- Isotretinoin and alcohol don't cause an instant dangerous reaction, but both raise **triglycerides** and put load on your **liver**.
- Many dermatologists advise avoiding alcohol during treatment. Others allow occasional light drinking if your bloodwork is normal. Ask yours.
- **Never binge** on isotretinoin, and skip alcohol for a few days before blood tests.
- If your triglycerides or liver enzymes are raised, don't drink until your doctor says it's fine.
- Expect worse dryness and possibly rougher hangovers. Hydrate well.
- Don't take vitamin A supplements, and check with your doctor before any liver or hangover supplement.
- Severe stomach pain, yellow skin or eyes, a severe headache with vision changes, or low mood with thoughts of self-harm need medical help right away.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol on Accutane?**

Many dermatologists recommend avoiding alcohol during an isotretinoin course, and others allow occasional light drinking if your blood tests are normal. There's no instant dangerous reaction, but alcohol and isotretinoin both raise triglycerides and add load to your liver. Ask your dermatologist what limit they want you to follow, never binge, and don't drink at all if your triglycerides or liver enzymes are raised.

**Does alcohol affect Accutane bloodwork?**

Yes. Alcohol can raise triglycerides and liver enzymes like ALT, AST, and GGT, and drinking in the few days before a blood test can make your results look worse than they really are. That can lead to repeat tests, a lower dose, or a pause in treatment. Skipping alcohol for at least two to three days before a test, following your fasting instructions, and being honest with your doctor about your drinking helps keep your results accurate.

**Why can't you drink on Accutane?**

The main reasons are triglycerides and the liver. Isotretinoin raises blood triglycerides in a significant share of patients, and alcohol raises them too, which increases the risk of very high levels and, rarely, pancreatitis. Both also put extra work on the liver, which your doctor monitors with blood tests. Alcohol can also make the dryness and mood side effects of isotretinoin feel worse.

**How long after Accutane can I drink alcohol?**

There's no official waiting period. Isotretinoin clears from the body within about a week of the last dose, and raised triglycerides and liver enzymes usually return to normal after treatment ends. If your blood results stayed normal during the course, many people go back to their usual drinking within a week or two. If any results were raised, wait until your doctor confirms they're back to normal.

**Are hangovers worse on Accutane?**

Many people find they are. Isotretinoin dries you out, can cause headaches, tiredness, and aches on its own, and may lower your mood, so the usual hangover symptoms can feel stronger. There isn't good research measuring this directly, but if your tolerance seems lower, drink less and hydrate more. A severe headache with blurred vision or vomiting is not a normal hangover on isotretinoin and needs a call to your doctor.

**Does alcohol make Accutane stop working?**

There's no good evidence that moderate drinking stops isotretinoin from clearing acne. The indirect risk is that drinking can raise your liver enzymes or triglycerides, which may lead your dermatologist to lower your dose or pause treatment, and that can slow your results.

**Can I take a liver or hangover supplement while on Accutane?**

Check with your dermatologist first. Never take vitamin A supplements on isotretinoin, and check multivitamins and hangover blends for vitamin A or retinol. Herbal liver products can affect liver enzymes themselves and make your blood results harder to read. There's no good evidence that DHM or any other supplement makes drinking on isotretinoin safe.

**Is it OK to drink on Accutane if my liver tests are normal?**

Normal results are reassuring, and some dermatologists will allow occasional light drinking in that situation. Keep it to one or two drinks with food, avoid binges and back-to-back nights, and skip alcohol before your next test. Your results can change during the course, so check in with your doctor if a later test comes back raised.
